newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Funds are a wild card in coffee's deck.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Funds are a wild card in coffee's deck.

text.p: Coffee nations in London talks on Tuesday mulled a warning that a speculative bubble that has lifted prices by 80-100 percent since January might collapse as dramatically as it began.

A report by officials of the International Coffee Organization (ICO) said world futures prices for green (unroasted) coffee beans could slump if speculative funds dump big positions that they have built up in the past few months.
"...With cumulative purchases by investment funds, there is always a possibility that a massive liquidation of positions could trigger large falls in prices," the ICO said.
Such a prospect is unlikely before the end of Brazil's winter which lasts through August, when there is always a risk of a damaging frost in the world's biggest grower.
But the speculative character of the rally in coffee, the longest unbroken run-up in two decades, fuelled concerns.

Nations that grow coffee are enjoying a windfall now, but fret about future volatility and a risk that, as roasters pass on the high cost of beans at the shops, consumers may switch to tea or soft drinks.
Reacting to this danger, the 14-nation Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC), meeting in London, is considering making export quotas more flexible, delegates said.

They said one idea is that producers would agree to meet again if prices rose to predetermined "trigger" levels. Coffee futures slipped a little this week on profit-taking but not before the expiring New York May contract for quality arabica beans had hit a 20-year high at $2.80 per pound.
"There's a concern that as the market approaches $3.00 you start to impact consumption," said Steve Platt, an analyst at Dean Witter in the United States.
"And producers don't want to shut off consumption."

The ACPC producers led by Brazil, the biggest, are talking in the margin of a week of discussions at the International Coffee Organization, the larger but mainly consultative body of 62 countries that also includes the consumers.
The ICO, in its report to delegates at the London talks, said world coffee supply had been below demand since 1993.
Also, stocks in the big coffee-drinking countries were down to seven million (60 kg) bags at the end of last year or only about one-third of levels early in the 1990s.
Roasters, who had been buying hand-to-mouth, might need to readjust their stocks, the ICO said.
It added that the rally in prices had also been fuelled by weather damage to crops and by labour unrest in Latin America.
But the market now expected adequate supplies of arabica coffee when the new 1997/98 crop is harvested in much of Latin America during the last quarter of 1997.
